name: Andersen-Tawil syndrome
aliases: periodic paralysis with cardiac dysrhythmia and dysmorphism

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Defined by a clinical triad of periodic paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia with characteristic electrocardiographic changes, and distinctive dysmorphic features
Dysmorphism includes low-set ears, hypertelorism, a small mandible, clinodactyly and syndactyly, and short stature
The characteristic electrocardiogram shows prominent U waves and a prolonged QU interval with frequent ventricular ectopy, and it is classed as long QT syndrome type 7
Ventricular arrhythmias, including bidirectional and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, are often surprisingly well tolerated but carry a risk of syncope
Periodic paralysis in this syndrome can be associated with a low, normal or high serum potassium, so the potassium-shift pattern is variable between families
Inherited as an autosomal dominant condition with marked variable expressivity, most often due to mutations in the KCNJ2 gene encoding the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1
The full triad may be incomplete in any given patient, so a normal cardiac or dysmorphic assessment does not exclude the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Andersen-Tawil syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in KCNJ2, which encodes the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1. This channel stabilises the resting membrane potential and shapes the terminal phase of repolarisation in both skeletal and cardiac muscle. Reduced Kir2.1 current, often through a dominant-negative effect on the tetrameric channel, destabilises the resting potential of skeletal muscle to produce periodic paralysis, and prolongs and destabilises cardiac repolarisation to generate the prominent U waves, QU prolongation and ventricular arrhythmias. The same channel and related developmental signalling pathways are implicated in the skeletal and craniofacial dysmorphism that completes the triad.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic causes of short stature and dysmorphism
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram and prolonged rhythm monitoring for U waves, QU prolongation and ventricular ectopy
Serum potassium measured during paralytic episodes
Echocardiography to assess cardiac structure and function
Prolonged exercise electromyography protocol to characterise the periodic paralysis
Targeted KCNJ2 genetic testing, with a broader panel if negative
Clinical dysmorphology assessment and skeletal imaging as indicated
redFlags: Syncope, palpitations or documented ventricular tachycardia indicating arrhythmic risk
Family history of sudden cardiac death
Marked QU prolongation with frequent or complex ventricular ectopy
Respiratory or severe generalised weakness during a paralytic attack
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually near normal because the ventricular arrhythmias are frequently well tolerated, but syncope and, rarely, sudden cardiac death can occur, so cardiac surveillance is essential and the periodic paralysis and dysmorphic features add variable long-term morbidity.
pitfalls: Diagnosing simple periodic paralysis and missing the cardiac and dysmorphic components of the triad
Expecting a consistent potassium-shift direction, when the potassium level during attacks is variable
Under-appreciating arrhythmic risk because the ventricular tachycardia is often asymptomatic
Prescribing QT-prolonging drugs without recognising the underlying repolarisation abnormality
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
